hints: A scramble preserves the multiset of characters in every corresponding substring.
Define a state by the two starting indices and the common substring length.
For each split, consider both keeping the two parts in order and swapping them.
Memoize states to avoid recomputing the same substring pairs.
title: Scramble String Problem

constraints: s1 and s2 consist of lowercase English letters.
content.inputFormat: Single line: JSON array of all arguments, e.g. [arg1, arg2, ...]

sampleTestCases.explanation: A valid sequence of splits and swaps transforms "great" into "rgeat", so the result is true.
Although both strings contain the same letters, no valid recursive split-and-swap sequence transforms "abcde" into "caebd", so the result is false.
For a one-character string, the only possible result is the original character, so the strings match.

content.problemStatement:
Task: We can scramble a string s to get a string t using the following algorithm:

1. If the length of the string is 1, stop.
2. If the length of the string is > 1, do the following:
   * Split the string into two non-empty substrings at a random index, i.e., if the string is `s`, divide it to `x` and `y` where `s = x + y`.
   * **Randomly** decide to swap the two substrings or to keep them in the same order. i.e., after this step, `s` may become `s = x + y` or `s = y + x`.
   * Apply step 1 recursively on each of the two substrings `x` and `y`.

You receive two strings `s1` and `s2` of **the same length**, output `true` if `s2` is a scrambled string of `s1`, otherwise, output `false`.

solution.approach: Use interval dynamic programming (memoized recursion). A state (i, j, len) asks whether the substring of s1 starting at i and the substring of s2 starting at j, both of length len, are scrambles. Before trying split points, compare character frequencies to prune impossible states. For every split k, check both the no-swap and swap partitions.

better.complexity: O(n^4) time and O(n^3) memo space.
better.description: Memoize each interval-pair state (i, j, len), so each state is solved once. Character-frequency pruning avoids exploring partitions whose substrings do not have the same multiset of letters.

optimal.complexity: O(n^4) time and O(n^3) auxiliary space.
optimal.description: Use the memoized interval DP above. For each state, check equality, character frequencies, and both partition orientations for every split point. This exactly captures the recursive scramble definition.

bruteForce.complexity: Exponential time in the worst case; recursion depth O(n).
bruteForce.description: Try every recursive split and both swap choices without memoization. This is correct but exponential because the same substring-pair states are recomputed many times.

followUps: Can you implement the same recurrence bottom-up?
How would the state space change if the alphabet were larger?
What practical pruning can reduce the number of states explored?
learningObjectives: Model recursive string transformations with interval dynamic programming.
Use memoization to remove overlapping subproblems.
Recognize when character-frequency checks safely prune DP states.
Analyze O(n^4) time and O(n^3) space for three-dimensional interval states.
